Associated with initial reduction, and at least partially responsible for it is a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems. In all Northern Paman languages, except Uraði and its sister dialects, *C1 was lost invariably. Even in Uraði the prevailing tendency has been toward initial loss, although *C1 is sometimes positively reflected in that language. new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement by the fieldworker covering all his Northern Paman varieties, Ŋkot̠ = Ngkoth included: primary stress is non-contrastive ('strictly phonetic') and sits on the reflex of the Proto-Paman second syllable, the old initial syllable having been reduced (initial consonant lost invariably in Ngkoth; initial short vowel lost, kept or metathesised). Synchronically this amounts to stress on the first consonant-initial syllable of the modern word (word-initial in the now common cluster-initial/monosyllabic stems, second syllable in vowel-initial words), which is exactly the rule Hale states explicitly for the sister language Linngithigh on p. 179 ('the first vowel which is preceded by a consonant is stressed'); Hale gives no separate synchronic stress rule for Ngkoth itself, either here or in the Ngkot section of his 1976a paper.
new_statements.exceptions: Uradhi and its sister dialects are excepted only with respect to invariable *C1 loss, not explicitly with respect to the stress shift; no Ngkoth-specific exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Diachronic/comparative statement about 'Paman stems' (word level); stress called 'a strictly phonetic feature', i.e. non-phonemic. No phrase-level information. Ngkoth data from one consultant (Frank Moreton), Weipa 1960.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is Hale's own first-hand generalisation over the whole Northern Paman subgroup (Glottolog nort2758 'Northern Paman'), of which Ŋkot̠ (= Ngkoth, ngko1236; consultant Frank Moreton, Weipa 1960) is one of his 13 sampled varieties (listed AL 8(2):163, described 165-166). It is not an Ngkoth-specific synchronic rule; Hale's Ngkot section in the fuller 1976a paper lists five 'major phonological developments' and none concerns stress. The only explicit synchronic stress rule Hale gives for a Northern Paman language in this source is for the sister language Linngithigh (linn1234), p. 179.

new_statements.quote: Most, but not all, of the ID languages assign the most prominent stress in the word according to the following principle: stress the first vowel that follows a consonant. With certain of the ID languages, those in which second vowels are always continued [sic, scanned] stressed, it is at least plausible that ID is a consequence of a prior shift of stress from the first to the second syllable and is an instance of stress-conditioned lenition [...]. These languages include the Thaypan group (Thaypan-Laya, Aghu-Tharnggala, Alwangara, Rarmul), the Lamalamic group (Barimangudinma, Umbuygamu and Lamalama), and the Northern Paman languages other than Uradhi-Yaraikana.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's Hale 1966 statement (stress shifted from initial to second syllable of Paman stems, = first post-consonantal vowel after initial C-loss); adds the synchronic formulation 'stress the first vowel that follows a consonant' and the explicit inclusion of Northern Paman other than Uradhi. Attribution to Alpher rather than Sutton 1976 rests on the paper opening chained from the same text, Blevins 2001's citation of Alpher 1976:86-7 for the Kunjen argument in this passage, and Sutton's later reference to 'the definition cited above'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In the initial-dropping (ID) languages, which by Alpher's own list include the Northern Paman languages other than Uradhi (so Ngkoth), main stress goes on the first vowel that follows a consonant; in these Northern Paman languages the (etymological) second vowel is always the stressed one, which Alpher takes as evidence that ID followed a shift of stress from the first to the second syllable. Group-level statement; Ngkoth is not named individually.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Most, but not all' ID languages follow the principle; Uradhi-Yaraikana excluded from the always-second-vowel set; Kunjen (Oykangand, Uw-El) keeps first-syllable stress and is argued to have undergone ID independently of stress shift; Umbindhamu may stress initial long vowels.
new_statements.identity_note: All three works treat Ngkoth only as a member of Northern Paman (Hale 1976a's Ngkot section, /ŋkot/, Weipa area, = McConnel's Nggot). Hale 1976b describes Uradhi (Mr Ducie's variety) and extends the stress rule to all Northern Paman; Alpher 1976 speaks of the initial-dropping languages collectively, naming the Northern Paman languages other than Uradhi-Yaraikana. The volume's other stress passages (Umbindhamu, p. 75; Proto-Paman 'initial (stressed) syllables', p. 73; a Kuuku-Ya'u-type descriptive phonology with primary/secondary stress) belong to other papers and other languages.

new_statements.quote: by means of a rule which is apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages, namely: V -+ V/#(V)Ci _ [scanned of V → V́ / #(V)C1 __] This is, stress the first post-consonantal vowel in the word. Hence, using the longer interpretation of the rule, /utaga/ [utagak"1] 'dog'. And using the shorter interpretation, /minhitji/ [mfnh i kY i k-1] 'bird'. Finally, a very noticeable feature in Uradhi is a vowel-deletion rule of the following form: V -* 0/ _ #V That is, a vowel is deleted word-finally if followed immediately by a word-initial vowel. Evidently, stress is assigned to words prior to the application of this vowel deletion rule.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (Hale 1966: primary stress on the erstwhile second syllable, = first post-consonantal vowel), now given as an explicit synchronic rule with a formal statement and claimed for all Northern Paman; describes Uradhi directly, Ngkoth only by the group-wide claim.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress the first post-consonantal vowel of the word (V → V́ / #(V)C __): initial vowel-initial words stress the second vowel, consonant-initial words the first. Stated for Uradhi but explicitly as a rule 'apparently shared by all of the Northern Paman languages', hence covering Ngkoth. Stress is assigned before Uradhi's word-final vowel deletion.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; 'apparently' hedges the group-wide claim. Note: the quote printed in the works list under this citation ('assign the most prominent stress.. stress the first vowel that follows a consonant') is actually Alpher 1976's wording, not Hale's.
